content: The sensitivity and specificity of diagnostic assays can vary significantly between different assays and even between studies evaluating the same assay. However, the clinical sensitivity of assays for detecting chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection is unlikely to be substantially reduced, as the majority of chronic HBV infections are associated with blood HBsAg concentrations well above 10 IU/mL. Nevertheless, it is critical to carefully select assays with minimal rates of false positivity, both analytically and clinically, to ensure accurate diagnosis. The Guidelines Development Group chose not to define minimum performance characteristics for assays but recommended that any assay used should meet the stringent performance criteria established by regulatory authorities, particularly in terms of analytical and clinical sensitivity and specificity. For example, the use of rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) or laboratory-based enzyme immunoassays (EIAs), chemiluminescence immunoassays (CLIAs), or electrochemiluminescence assays (ECLs) for detecting HBsAg should adhere to the minimum performance standards set by the World Health Organization (WHO) prequalification of in vitro diagnostics (IVDs) or stringent regulatory reviews. All IVDs must be used according to the manufacturer’s instructions and, where possible, in testing sites enrolled in national or international external quality assessment schemes. The rationale for these recommendations is based on a balance of benefits and harms. For instance, a one-assay serological testing strategy for diagnosing chronic HBV infection is conditionally recommended based on low-quality evidence. This approach efficiently identifies most individuals likely to be infected and in need of further evaluation while ruling out uninfected individuals. Although this strategy may generate some false-positive results, the clinical consequences are considered negligible, as no patient would be initiated on lifelong antiviral therapy based solely on a single serological test. In many settings, it is common practice to perform a second test after six months to confirm a diagnosis of chronic HBV and distinguish it from acute hepatitis B. This additional step provides further confirmation of chronic infection. If the initial test has high specificity, very few individuals would require a second test, simplifying the testing process and reducing costs, especially when testing is delivered at the point of care. Rapid reporting of test results, ideally on the same day, can improve access to care and linkage to treatment. In low-prevalence settings, a two-assay testing strategy may be necessary to improve the positive predictive value (PPV). A single serological assay, even with 99% specificity, may yield more false-positive than true-positive results in such settings. In these cases, confirmation with a neutralization step or a second, different assay is recommended. However, the added value of a second RDT has been minimally evaluated, and challenges exist, such as the potential for similar inaccuracies across different RDT brands and the risk of missing true HBsAg-positive individuals if the assay’s sensitivity is poor. For hepatitis C virus (HCV) testing, serological assays are used to detect evidence of past or present infection. These assays, which include RDTs and laboratory-based immunoassays, must meet minimum safety, quality, and performance standards. In settings with limited laboratory infrastructure, RDTs are recommended due to their simplicity, low cost, and rapid turnaround time. They are particularly useful in hard-to-reach populations and rural areas, as they do not require extensive laboratory infrastructure or equipment. A single serological assay is recommended for initial detection of HCV antibodies, followed by nucleic acid testing (NAT) to confirm viremic infection. This approach is cost-effective and minimizes the number of individuals referred for more expensive NAT technologies. In children under 18 months of age, HCV infection can only be confirmed using virological assays to detect HCV RNA, as maternal antibodies may persist in the child’s bloodstream, rendering serological results ambiguous. The performance of RDTs and EIAs for HCV antibody detection has been evaluated across various populations and settings. RDTs generally demonstrate high sensitivity and specificity, comparable to laboratory-based EIAs. However, RDTs using oral fluid have slightly lower sensitivity but higher specificity compared to those using blood specimens. The OraQuick ADVANCE® HCV Rapid Antibody Test, for example, has shown higher sensitivity compared to other brands. In resource-limited settings, the use of RDTs is preferred due to their simplicity, affordability, and ability to provide same-day results, which reduces the need for follow-up appointments and improves linkage to care. In contrast, laboratory-based EIAs may be more appropriate in settings with existing laboratory infrastructure and high testing volumes, as they are cost-effective and suitable for large-scale testing. The latest generation of assays for HCV antibody detection also includes the capability to detect HCV core antigen (HCVcAg), which improves assay sensitivity and reduces the diagnostic window period. This advancement enhances the ability to detect recent HCV infections and supports timely diagnosis and treatment.
